title: Chapter 157 – Seven Beds
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Lin Jian]

The Annex lies at the very center of the dome, and they walk to it in silence along a ring of light that runs down through the terraces like the spoke of a wheel.

Jian does not use his staff. He leans on it. He has stopped pretending, now, that it is for anything else. The long pale gown that Nurse gave him drags around his ankles and the slippers are too large. His knees ache with a dull steady burn, and when he looks at his hands, which are folded on the staff's crook, they are a stranger's: freckled, ridged, the veins standing up like cords. A hundred and nineteen. He says the number to himself like a lesson, and finds that it means nothing at all.

Brother, says the boy, from the room.

Yes.

You're slowing down.

I know.

It's all right. We can stop. A pause. Please can we stop? I want to see them, but I'm scared to.

He halts. Behind him Bell stops, and Yue, and Nurse, walking ahead in her silent slippers, turns with a small inquiring tilt of the head. He puts both hands on the crook of the staff and takes three deep breaths of the cool sweet air.

"A moment," he says. "Please."

"Of course." Nurse inclines her head. "There is no hurry. They are not going anywhere."

It is a gentle joke. It lands wrongly. Bell makes a small strangled sound. But Jian finds that it steadies him, a little, and he lifts his head and looks at the blue distance and says, "How far?"

"Fifty paces."

He nods. He closes his eyes, and lets the boy come forward, and the two of them walk the last of the way together.

* * *

The Annex is a small round room.

It is not what he expected. After the vastness of the dome, the endless terraces, the cold blue immensity of two hundred thousand sleepers, he had imagined a chamber of the same kind. But it is small. It might be the size of the common room in the old house, with a low ceiling and warm lamplight and a floor of soft pale wood. The walls curve gently in. There is a window, high up, with no view in it, only a patch of dim gold. It smells faintly of apples.

He stops in the door.

There are seven beds.

They are not cradles. That is the first thing he sees. They are real beds, low and plain, of dark wood and white linen, arranged in a half circle around a small stove. The stove is cold. On top of it stands a kettle. Beside each bed there is a table, and on each table a lamp, and each lamp is lit.

In the beds, asleep, lie seven children.

He does not move. He cannot. The air has gone very still. Behind him, Bell draws a sharp breath. Yue's hand finds his sleeve.

Oh, says the boy, in a voice so small that it is hardly a sound. Oh. Oh.

* * *

They lie in a row, the youngest at the left.

The first is a girl of three. She is small and round-faced and brown, with her thumb in her mouth and a tangle of black curls on the pillow, and one fat fist closed around the ear of a stuffed rabbit that has been mended many times. The label on the foot of the bed says, in a round careful hand: AO. Operator 1. Aged three years, two months.

The second is a boy of five, thin and solemn, with a gap in his front teeth and a wooden top held loosely against his chest. TAO. Operator 7.

The third is a girl of eight. She sleeps with her mouth shut tight, even in sleep, and her small sharp face is turned to the wall as if she were refusing to hear. There is a charcoal drawing pinned above her bed, a crude scribble of a house and a tree and seven stick figures. MO YAN. Operator 6.

The fourth is a boy of eleven with a shock of straight hair and a small brass lamp clenched in one hand. The fifth, fourteen, has dirt under his fingernails and a face brown from the sun. The sixth, sixteen, lies with a sword-hilt across his chest and a scar on his upper lip. The seventh, nineteen, the eldest, wears the plain gray of the Court, and has a book open on his chest, as though he had fallen asleep reading.

The labels say, in order, ZHEN LI. Operator 5. HAI REN. Operator 4. DUAN KE. Operator 3. CHENG HUI. Operator 2. And at the far end of the row, in an iron frame, with fresh linen and a new lamp and a name on the foot that has been written and rubbed out and written again until the paper is thin:

LIN JIAN. Operator 8. Reserved.

The bed is empty.

* * *

Bell is the first to move. She is across the room before he has found his voice, down on one knee beside the smallest bed, with her satchel dropped on the floor and two fingers on the little girl's wrist. Her face is white and absorbed and entirely professional.

"Pulse is slow. Thirty. Thirty-two." Her lips move. "Skin is warm. No dehydration. No wasting. She looks as though she went to sleep last night." She lays her palm on the child's brow. "She is perfect. Jian, she is perfect. I don't understand it."

"She has been asleep for six hundred years," says Nurse, softly, from the door.

"I know what you said." Bell does not look round. "I'm telling you what I see."

"You see the effect of the Hall. The cradles hold their occupants in stasis. The beds do not. The beds are something else." Nurse's slippers whisper on the boards. "Operator Five built them. They are not for sleeping. They are for keeping. The children are not asleep. They are held."

"Held?"

"The way a breath is held." She stops at the foot of Ao's bed and lays a hand on the rail. "When the Operator died, the Gate did what it was designed to do. It took the stored copy and sent it across, and the working copy was lost. But the child was still present. The Gate could not discard a living pattern. It was not in the design." A pause. "So it brought them here. One by one. And Operator Five, who was Ethan Cole, built the beds."

Jian takes a step forward. His voice, when it comes, is a rasp. "He knew they were alive."

"He knew from the first."

"And he left them asleep."

"He could not wake them. The Gate would not allow it. A child has to be asked." The brown eyes are very bright. "He sat with them every night for six years. I have the record. He read to them. He told them the names of the stars. When he died, the Gate took him too, and it was Operator Six, and Seven, and so on, and each of them visited, and left a gift. A toy. A top. A book." She lifts a hand to the row of tables. "You see?"

He does see. On Ao's table, beside the lamp, lies a stuffed rabbit with a red scarf. On Tao's, a spinning top. On Mo Yan's, a bundle of charcoal sticks. A brass lamp. A string of beads. A hilt. A book. Each one worn smooth, as if a thumb had turned it over a thousand times.

They came to visit, says the boy. His voice is thick. They came every year. And they couldn't wake us.

No.

They were so sorry.

I know.

I wish I'd known. A small, hiccuping breath. I wish I could tell them it's all right.

He cannot answer. He puts a hand over his eyes.

* * *

The boy asks to go to the beds.

He does it without ceremony, as he does everything: a shy, plain tug at the front of Jian's mind, and then the old white-haired body is walking down the row, slowly, with the staff left leaning against the stove. The boy walks as Jian never has, with a lightness in the step and his head turned a little to the left, looking at each of the sleepers in turn. He stops at Ao's bed. He crouches beside it, with a creak of the knee, and gently touches the stuffed rabbit's mended ear.

"Hello," he says. His voice is hardly more than a whisper. "I'm Lin Jian. I'm the eighth. I'm sorry I'm late."

Ao does not stir.

He goes on, bed to bed. At Tao's he says hello. At Mo Yan's he pauses a long time, and lays one finger lightly against the edge of the charcoal drawing pinned to the wall. At the foot of the boy with the brass lamp he stands very still, and says, "I think you're afraid of the dark. It's all right. I am too." At the sixth bed he reads the label twice and laughs a little, shakily, because the sleeper is sixteen and has a sword on his chest and looks as though he would cheerfully knock the boy's head off. He stops last at the eldest, the scholar in the plain gray, with the book open on his chest, and bends to read the title.

It is a book of poems. It is open to a page that has been marked with a strip of red silk.

He reads aloud, softly, in his clear young voice, and Jian, behind his eyes, hears him with a tight painful wonder. It is not a good poem. It is a country song about a boy who goes to look for the moon and comes home with a stone in his pocket. But the boy reads it as though it were scripture.

When he has finished he closes the book, gently, on the strip of silk, and sets it on the table beside the lamp.

"Thank you," he says, to the sleeping scholar. "For keeping my place."

Nobody speaks. In the corner, Yue is crying openly, without sound. Bell has her face in her hands.

* * *

It is Yue who finds the first anomaly.

She has gone quietly down the row, with Pebble in her arms, laying her palm flat on the frame of each bed. Jian watches her with the dull absorbed curiosity of exhaustion. She stops at the fifth, the boy of fourteen. Her fingers tighten on the wood. Then she hurries to the sixth, and the seventh, and back again, and he sees her face go through three changes in as many seconds, puzzlement, then fear, then a kind of desperate hope.

Slate, she signs.

He hands it to her. She scrawls, and holds it up.

Five of them hum. Together. A chord. It's quiet and very faint but it's there. The two on the left do not.

The two youngest? he writes.

Yes. Ao and Tao. Nothing. Her hand shakes. No hum. No seam. Like stones.

Bell has gone rigid. She is on her knees beside Ao's bed with her ear against the child's chest, and when she lifts her head her face is the color of paper.

"Thirty," she says. "Thirty-two. It is not a heartbeat. It's an echo. It is a heartbeat's shape. There is nothing inside it." Her voice cracks. "Nurse. Is she dead?"

"No." Nurse has come across the room. She stands very straight, and her smooth face is quite calm, but her hands are clenched in her gown. "No, Doctor. She is failing."

"What does that mean?"

"The beds are fed from the same line as the cradles. The youngest are the weakest. They have the least pattern to sustain." The brown eyes close. "In the last month the draw to Annex Seven has dropped by half. I have been diverting power from the cradles to hold the children. I should not have done it. I could not stop."

"How long?"

"For Ao and Tao?" A flat, steady voice. "Six days. Perhaps seven."

Jian feels the floor tilt. He puts out a hand and finds the end of Mo Yan's bed, and holds on.

Six days, says the boy, in the room, very quietly. We've got six days.

* * *

Before they leave the Annex, Nurse plays them the record.

She does it hesitantly, standing at the stove, with one hand pressed flat against the wall as though listening for a pulse. "I should not," she says. "It is the last thing he asked me not to do. But I think you ought to hear it."

A sound fills the room. It is faint at first, a soft crackle like fire. Then a voice. A man's, low and tired and very kind, reading aloud, with the careful unhurried rhythm of someone who has read the same book a hundred times.

"...and so the little boy put the stone in his pocket and walked home along the river. It was a long way. His feet were cold. But the moon went with him the whole way, and when he got home he put the stone on the sill, and the moon looked in at the window, and said, I see you have my friend."

A pause. A soft dry laugh.

That's the end of that one. Do you want another? I know you're all asleep. I don't mind. I like the sound of my own voice.

Silence. A chair creaks.

Tao, I brought your top. It's not the same one. I'm sorry; the old one broke. Mo Yan, I can't tell if you hear me, but I'm going to say it anyway. I love your drawing. The tree is excellent. I think the seven figures are us. I think you're right.

Another pause, longer. When he speaks again his voice is thick.

I'm going to be dead soon, you know. Not forever. I've arranged for someone to come after me. A man very like me. He'll be bad at this, I should warn you. He won't know your names. A shaky breath. But he'll learn. He'll sit where I'm sitting and he'll say hello. And one of these years, one of you will say it back.

The recording crackles. There is a long soft hiss, and then it stops.

Nobody speaks. In the corner, Yue has her hands pressed to her mouth. She did not hear a word, but she read the faces, and that was enough.

"That was Operator Five," says Nurse gently. "In the sixth year. The year he died."

Jian's voice is a thread. "He knew he would die."

"He arranged it. He built the Dock to carry his memory forward. He built me." She lifts her head. "He asked me to keep the lamps lit. I have done so."

Every one of them, says the boy, quietly, in the room. All six hundred years.

* * *

They sit in the Annex until the lamps burn low.

No one suggests leaving. It does not seem possible. Bell has unpacked her satchel and laid out her instruments in a neat row on the stove: stethoscope, thermometer, lancets, the little glass vial of clear spirit. She works methodically, bed to bed, taking temperatures, counting breaths, writing numbers on the slate in the careful hand she uses for case notes. She does not speak. Yue has curled up on the floor at the foot of Ao's bed with her back against the frame and her cloak over Pebble. She has not taken her eyes off the little girl's face.

Jian sits on a stool in the middle of the room. He has nothing to do. The boy has retreated into the quiet of the little round room behind his eyes, and the two of them keep company in a long exhausted silence. Beyond the high window the gold light is fading. Somewhere very far off, in the dome, he can hear a faint slow sound like the tolling of a bell underwater. He thinks it is the sleepers. He thinks it is two hundred thousand hearts.

I could feed them, he thinks.

No.

Not the cradles. Only the children. Two of them. A week's worth. It would cost me—

No, says the boy, with a sharpness that startles him. You'll die.

I am going to die anyway.

Not yet. The small voice shakes. Not before I've met them. Not before we've done it right. You promised.

I did.

Then you can't.

He opens his mouth to answer, and cannot. Across the room Nurse stands at the stove with her back to them, motionless, looking at the cold kettle. He understands, suddenly and with a pang of pity, that she has stood like that every evening for twenty-five years.

"Nurse," he says, gently.

"Sir."

"Is there someone I ought to speak to? Someone who knows what to do?"

She does not turn. But her shoulders move, very slightly, in a way that is almost a shiver.

"There is," she says.

"Who?"

"He has been asking for you for three days."

* * *

The status line wakes while he is sitting there.

He has stopped expecting it. For forty-one days the little gray thread in the corner of his eye has said the same two words, Searching, and counted the days like a prisoner scratching a wall. He sees it change from the corner of his eye and for a moment does not understand. Then the characters resolve, one by one, in the faint gray of the old Interface, and his heart gives a great slow thump.

Nine months, he thinks.

Less, says the boy. If you step.

If I step. He reads it once more. Ethan's machine has told me how much time I have, in the kindest possible language. He almost laughs. I suppose it is a courtesy.

It isn't funny.

No.

The boy is silent for a moment. Then, in a very small voice: Do you want to stop?

Stop what?

All of it. Go home. Be old in the orchard, and eat Mama's soup. I'd like that. I think I'd like it more than anything. A shaky breath. But I don't think you'd be happy.

I would be very happy.

You'd be sad. Under it. The small voice is gentle. You'd listen to the Mother Tree every night, and know that two of them were still asleep.

He sits with that. The stove ticks. Far off, in the dome, the faint slow bell tolls.

I will try to do this without dying, he says at last.

That's all I want.

I will try very hard.

I know. The boy leans against him, in the quiet room. You always do.

* * *

Bell goes down the row with her satchel open, and Jian watches her work.

She does not hurry. She kneels at each bed in turn, lays two fingers against the sleeper's throat, and counts under her breath, her lips moving. She lifts an eyelid with her thumb. She presses a palm to a small chest and holds it there, head bent, listening with her whole body, the way she listens to a failing patient in the infirmary at home.

"Zhen Li, steady," she murmurs. "Hai Ren, steady. The sword boy, steady, and his hands are warm, which is good. The scholar..." She frowns. "Slow. Slower than a man of nineteen should be. But even."

She comes to Tao and stays there a long time.

"Cold fingers," she says at last. "Cold feet. The pulse is a thread, and it skips. I have seen this in the very old, in the last week." Her voice is flat, professional, and her hand on the small wrist is not. "And the little one is the same."

"Six days," says Jian.

"Perhaps seven, if nobody breathes on them." She sits back on her heels. "I can ease them. A little warmth, a little ginseng broth through a reed, if the throat will take it. It will not cure them. It will buy an hour here and an hour there."

"Then buy the hours."

"I will." She looks up at him, and her eyes go over his gray face, the hollows under his cheekbones, the hand he has laid flat on the bedpost to keep from swaying. "And you will sit down, Lin Jian, before I have to add you to the row."

He sits. It is not obedience. His knees simply stop.

* * *

Yue finds Nurse at the slate.

It is a long black slab set into the wall beside the stove, scrawled with white chalk in a hand that is neat and small and has been wiped and rewritten many times. Yue stands before it with her arms folded and her head tilted, reading, and now and then she lifts the chalk from the ledge and writes a question underneath.

Where does the power come from?

Nurse reads it over her shoulder, and answers in the same slow white letters.

From the Gate. Through the deep conduit. The beds, the lamps, the air, the water all drink from it.

And the Gate is failing.

The Gate was fed on names. Eight thousand years of names, burned one by one. Then a man named Ye returned four thousand, all at once. The Hall has been starving ever since.

Yue stares at that for a long moment. Her mouth tightens. She knows who stood beside Ye when it happened. She wipes the line with the heel of her hand, which leaves a white smear on her palm, and writes:

So the children are starving because of what we did.

Nurse does not hurry to console her. She takes the chalk, and writes, with great gentleness, one word.

Yes.

A silence. Then, underneath, smaller:

And also because of what was done before. Both are true. I cannot tell you which weighs more. I am sorry. I am only a nurse.

Yue reads it twice. Then she sets the chalk down very carefully, as though it might break, and walks to the nearest bed, and sits on its edge, and takes the sleeping hand of a boy of eleven in both of hers.

She does not write anything else. She cannot hear the lamps, or the bell, or the faint wet breath of the sleeper. But her shoulders, slowly, stop shaking.

* * *

The voice comes out of the stove.

Not the stove. The wall behind it. A small round grille that he had taken for a vent, set into the plaster at the height of a man's chest, begins to hum, and then to crackle, and then to speak. It is faint, tinny, distorted, the voice of a man calling from the bottom of a well. It is a mild tired kind voice, with a slight catch in it, and it says, over and over, in the manner of someone who has been saying it for a very long time:

Is anyone there? Is anyone there? Please. Is the child there?

Jian is on his feet. He does not remember rising. He has crossed the floor in three strides, with the pale gown tangled round his legs, and is standing before the grille with his hands out in front of him as though it were a fire.

Please. I think I heard the door. I think someone's come. Is it— is that—

"Mr. Cole," says Jian, hoarsely.

A pause. A long pause, full of static, and the faint dry rustle of a man trying to draw breath.

Lin Jian?

It is the boy who answers. Jian does not choose it. A soft rush in his chest, and his mouth opens on its own, and a high clear voice comes out of it, breaking, laughing and weeping at once.

"Yes. Hello. It's me. We're here."

A sound from the grille. Not words. A kind of hoarse choked cry, and then silence, and then, so quietly that Jian has to bend close to hear, a voice that has been rehearsing this for six hundred years and has lost every word of it.

Oh, says Ethan Cole. Oh, thank God. You came.

Please. Come to the center. I can't hold her any longer.
